tip: sollen marks an order or expectation coming from someone else, not a personal need. Wir sollen leiser sein = we are told to be quieter.
sich beeilen is reflexive, so it needs the pronoun uns. English hurry has none: Wir müssen uns beeilen.
warm here describes the verb, not a noun, so it stays uninflected: dich warm anziehen = to dress warmly.
A modal like kann takes second place and pushes the main verb to the clause end as an infinitive: kann ... tippen.
nicht wahr tacked onto the end is a tag question, like isn't it or right. Schönes Wetter heute, nicht wahr?
After das, der or die in the nominative singular, the adjective ends in -e: das kalte Wasser.
After ein with a neuter noun, the adjective takes -es: ein kaltes Bier.
Accusative masculine turns ein into einen and the adjective into -en: einen langen Weg.
gern has irregular comparison: gern, lieber, am liebsten (most of all). Sie trinkt ... am liebsten.
dürfen means to be allowed to, so darfst signals permission, not ability: Du darfst dir ein Eis aussuchen.
Adding -in makes a female agent noun: Mathematiker becomes Mathematikerin.
Repeated time spans go in the accusative with no preposition: jeden Morgen = every morning.
German has hunger rather than being hungry: Hunger haben, negated as keinen Hunger.
dieser takes the same endings as der, das, die, so neuter is dieses: dieses Formular.
Darf ich ...? is the polite formula for asking permission to do something: Darf ich Ihnen meinen Mann vorstellen?
Masculine and neuter nouns add -s in the genitive: Konzert becomes dieses Konzerts (of this concert).
werden plus the past participle makes the passive: muss unterschrieben werden = must be signed.
For a fixed location auf takes the dative: auf dem Berg = on the hill, no movement involved.
teils ..., teils ... pairs two partial statements: partly one way, partly the other. Teils interessant, teils langweilig.
